messages.text: I'm 70 years old, my Social Security is $1,900. My friend said I make too much for food stamps. Is that right?

Not necessarily. Your friend may be thinking of the general income limit, but households with someone 60 or older are treated differently. You could still qualify for food assistance (SNAP), so it's worth checking.

**Why $1,900 may not be too much**
- The general "gross" limit for one person is about $1,729 a month. That is before deductions. ([Propel's summary of the 2026–27 federal limits](https://www.propel.app/snap/snap-2026-2027-cola-increase/))
- Households with someone 60 or older usually skip that test. They only have to pass the "net" test, which is income after deductions. The net limit for one person is about $1,330 a month. (I couldn't open USDA's own pages, so these figures are from Propel. I haven't confirmed the 60+ rule on an official page.)
- Your income is above $1,330 before deductions. Deductions can bring it down, though. There's a standard deduction of about $217. Rent, utility costs, and medical bills can also count.
- Tennessee's limit is also unsettled. The official limit is 130% of poverty. Some recent reports say the state is moving to 200%. I couldn't confirm which one applies right now. [(Hoodline, June 2026)](https://hoodline.com/2026/06/snap-shakeup-could-put-more-food-on-memphis-tables/) and [(Sycamore Institute)](https://sycamoretn.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap-in-tennessee.pdf) disagree. If 200% applies, you could be under the limit either way.

So right now it looks **possible**, but I need a few details to say more. The most you could get for one person is about $306 a month. The amount depends on your costs.

1. About how much do you pay each month for rent or a mortgage?
2. Do you pay for heating or cooling separately? Also, roughly how much do you pay each month in medical bills, including your Medicare premium and prescriptions?

**How to apply, even while you're unsure**
- Online: [onedhs.tn.gov/csp](https://onedhs.tn.gov/csp)
- Phone: 1-833-772-8347 (TTY 711). Interpreters are available.
- Source: [Tennessee Department of Human Services SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)
- You can also call 211 for free local help with applying.

This is only a first look. Only the Department of Human Services can decide if you qualify. It costs nothing to apply.

Rent is $700 a month. I pay my own heat and AC, but I'm not sure of the exact amount since it changes with the seasons. For medical stuff, I'm out about $300 a month for prescriptions and copays. I don't know offhand what my Medicare premium is.

Thanks, that helps. It now looks **possible**, and maybe even likely, that you'd get some food assistance (SNAP). The amount would probably be small. Here's how I got there.

**How I worked it out (rough estimate)**
- Your income before taxes is $1,900. SNAP takes off a standard deduction of about $217. ([Propel's summary of the 2026–27 federal figures](https://www.propel.app/snap/snap-2026-2027-cola-increase/))
- **Medical costs:** SNAP counts medical costs over $35 a month for people 60 and older.
  - Your $300 in prescriptions and copays counts.
  - Your Medicare Part B premium counts too. The standard Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90, according to CMS's notice in the Federal Register. I only saw that in search results and didn't open the notice. Your Social Security letter will show your exact amount.
  - With the premium, your medical deduction is roughly $465.
- **Rent and utilities:** Your $700 rent counts. Because you pay heat and AC, Tennessee adds a set utility amount instead of your real bills. Your seasonal bills don't matter. I couldn't find that amount, so I can't give you an exact number.

**What that means**
- If your medical deduction includes the Medicare premium, your income after deductions comes out well under the roughly $1,330 limit for one person. That's true even with a low guess for the utility amount.
- If the premium doesn't count, you could land right near or over the limit. So the premium matters.
- The monthly amount would likely fall between the $25 minimum and about $100 or a bit more. That's only an estimate. The most one person can get is about $306.
- Tennessee's income limit is still unsettled (130% or 200% of poverty). At 200%, your chances look even better. I couldn't confirm which one applies.

**Two quick questions**
1. Is the $1,900 the amount before your Medicare premium comes out, or the amount that lands in your bank account?
2. Roughly how much do you have in savings and bank accounts? You don't have to say. Savings limits may apply, and I couldn't confirm Tennessee's current rule.

**How to apply**
- Online: [onedhs.tn.gov/csp](https://onedhs.tn.gov/csp)
- Phone: 1-833-772-8347 (TTY 711)
- Source: [Tennessee Department of Human Services SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)
- Free local help: call 211.

When you apply, list your Medicare premium, your medical bills, and your rent. Keep receipts or statements for them. Report everything accurately. Only the Department of Human Services can decide if you qualify. It costs nothing to apply, and you can still apply even if the numbers look close.
Hmm, I think the Medicare premium gets taken out of my check before it hits my bank. Not totally sure though. The $1,900 is what I get from Social Security. And I have about $3,500 in savings.

Thanks. Your answers make it look a bit better. It's still **possible**, not certain, because I couldn't confirm Tennessee's set utility amount.

**Why the premium question matters less now**
- SNAP counts your Social Security **before** the Medicare premium is taken out. Your award letter or Social Security statement shows that "gross" amount.
- If the $1,900 is already after the premium, your real gross is about $2,100. If $1,900 is the gross, the premium is already inside it.
- Either way, the premium counts as a medical cost. Together with your $300 in prescriptions and copays, that's roughly $465 a month in medical deductions.

**Estimate for each case**
- **If $1,900 is your gross:** after the deductions, your income lands well under the roughly $1,330 limit. A rough guess is about $25 to $90 a month.
- **If your gross is about $2,100:** you'd still likely pass the income test. It depends on the utility amount Tennessee uses for heating and cooling, which I couldn't find. You'd probably get closer to the $25 minimum.
- These are rough estimates, not a promise. The most one person can get is about $306 a month. ([Propel's summary of the 2026–27 federal figures](https://www.propel.app/snap/snap-2026-2027-cola-increase/))

**Your savings**
- $3,500 is probably fine. A search result said the savings limit is $4,500 for households with someone 60 or older. I didn't open an official page to confirm that. Tennessee may also be changing its savings rules, so a caseworker will check.

**Next steps**
1. Find your Social Security award letter or statement. It shows your gross benefit and your Part B premium.
2. Apply:
   - Online: [onedhs.tn.gov/csp](https://onedhs.tn.gov/csp)
   - Phone: 1-833-772-8347 (TTY 711)
   - Source: [Tennessee Department of Human Services SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)
3. Have your rent, a recent utility bill, and your medical receipts ready.
4. For free help applying, call 211.

If your premium is taking a big bite of your check, ask 211 or TennCare about help paying Medicare costs. I haven't checked those programs for you.

Only the Department of Human Services can decide if you qualify. Please report everything accurately. It costs nothing to apply.

I didn't find any FY2027 figure for a one-person household's net income limit. The search turned up FY2026 numbers and a conflicting report about a policy change.

- **Net test:** Tennessee's net income test is 100% of the federal poverty level, and the 1-person FY2026 gross limit is $1,696 per month. Households with an elderly member (60+) or a disabled person only need to meet the net income test, not the gross income test.
- **Conflicting policy report:** A June 2026 Hoodline article says the Tennessee Department of Human Services has adopted broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE), which raises the SNAP gross-income threshold from 130% to 200% of total household gross monthly income and removes asset limits for some households. A January 2026 Sycamore Institute report instead said that pending approval from the Tennessee General Assembly, TDHS is in the process of changing state-level BBCE rules. I couldn't confirm which is current, so this needs checking against TDHS.
- **Asset limits:** One source says the SNAP asset limit is $3,000 for most households and goes up to $4,500 if your household includes at least one senior (60+) or disabled person. Those figures may predate the BBCE change.

The best next step is the official TDHS SNAP eligibility page or the USDA FY2027 income eligibility standards, which should give the exact net limit for one person.

The search turned up the official USDA memo, but the snippets don't include the FY 2027 income eligibility limits or standard deduction amounts.

**What's confirmed:**
- USDA's FY 2027 COLA memo, dated August 21, 2026, sets the new figures, which take effect October 1, 2026. In accordance with the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, the COLAs are effective as of October 1, 2026.
- Maximum allotment for a family of four in the 48 states and D.C. is $1,023, up from $994. Other household sizes: $306 for one person, $562 for two, $808 for three, and $1,217 for five (per Propel's table of 2026–2027 figures).
- Hawaii is the exception: the maximum allotment for a family of four in Hawaii will decrease to $1,655.
- The minimum benefit for the 48 States and D.C. will increase to $25.
- The shelter cap value will increase to $769 for the 48 States and D.C.
- For FY 2027, this caps the maximum allotment for households with 18 or more persons at $3,887 in the 48 States and the District of Columbia.

**Gaps and conflicts:**
- Income eligibility standards and standard deduction amounts were not in the retrieved text. The USDA memo's attachment cut off before those tables, so they need to be checked directly in the PDF.
- One secondary source gives the period as running through Sept. 20, 2027, while the USDA memo and other coverage say September 30, 2027. The USDA date is the one to rely on.

**How to apply for SNAP in Tennessee**

- **Online:** Apply through the One DHS Customer Portal at onedhs.tn.gov/csp, available 24/7. You can apply from a phone, tablet, or computer.
- **Printed application:** Mail or upload a printed application to TDHS. You can ask your local office to mail one to you, or download one in your language from the Applying for Services page.
- **Phone:** Call the One DHS Contact Center at +1-833-772-8347 (TDHS). For TTY, dial 711. Interpreters are available.
- **Help from outreach partners:** TDHS SNAP Outreach partners can provide pre-screening and application help.
- **In person:** Visit a TDHS Family Assistance office. In Davidson County, SNAP services are moving to the Antioch office at 5216 Hickory Hollow Parkway.

**Verification documents to gather**

Submitting these within 10 days of applying can help avoid delays:
- Social Security number
- Identification
- Proof of residence
- Income
- Resources (such as bank statements)
- Shelter costs
- Utility costs

**Not covered on this page**

The page does not include information on income limits, elderly or disabled household rules, resource limits, or broad-based categorical eligibility. For those details, see the Eligibility Information page on the TDHS site, or contact the One DHS Contact Center or SnapPolicy.DHS@tn.gov.

The CMS-announced 2026 standard Part B premium is $202.90 per month, up from $185.00 in 2025. The official Federal Register notice confirms the figure. The 2026 premium is 9.7 percent or $17.90 higher than the 2025 standard premium rate.

- **Deductible:** The annual Part B deductible rises to $283 in 2026, up from $257 in 2025 (the Part B deductible for 2026 is $283.00 for all Part B beneficiaries).
- **Actuarial rates:** The Federal Register notice lists $405.40 for aged enrollees and $548.60 for disabled enrollees. A Benzinga article gives $585.60 for disabled enrollees, so that figure conflicts with the official notice. I'd rely on the Federal Register.
- **Cause:** CMS attributed the increase to projected price changes and assumed utilization increases that are consistent with historical experience.
- **Income-related surcharges:** Higher-income beneficiaries pay more. Their total premiums are about 35, 50, 65, 80, or 85 percent of Part B costs, depending on income tier (per the Federal Register notice).
